q: Which statement best describes the role of hormones in relation to physical activity?
options: Hormones only influence reproductive processes in the body.
Hormones influence muscular development, energy, metabolism and reproductive processes.
Hormones alone determine whether an athlete performs successfully.
Hormones influence only athletes competing at elite levels.
feedback: Hormones influence several body functions relevant to physical activity, but their effects vary between individuals.

q: Which statement about the menstrual cycle is most accurate?
options: Every menstrual cycle lasts exactly 28 days.
Menstruation occurs after the luteal phase and is completely separate from the follicular phase.
Cycle length and individual experiences can vary.
Hormone levels remain constant throughout the cycle.
feedback: A 28-day cycle is a simplified model; cycle length and experiences can vary.

q: What occurs during ovulation?
options: The lining of the uterus is shed.
An egg is released from an ovary.
Progesterone immediately reaches its lowest level.
Menstruation begins at the same time.
feedback: Ovulation involves the release of an egg from the ovary.

q: Which hormone typically rises during the luteal phase?
options: Progesterone
Insulin
Adrenaline
Testosterone only
feedback: Progesterone rises during the luteal phase.

q: Which description best defines period poverty?
options: Having changes in the timing of the menstrual cycle.
Having inadequate access to menstrual products, facilities, education or support.
Experiencing pain or discomfort during menstruation.
Choosing to reduce physical activity during menstruation.
feedback: Period poverty involves practical and educational barriers to managing menstruation.

q: Amenorrhea refers to:
options: excessive menstrual bleeding.
menstrual pain during physical activity.
the absence of menstruation.
increased energy during the menstrual cycle.
feedback: Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation and can require appropriate medical assessment.

q: Which group best represents the three linked areas of the Female Athlete Triad?
options: Low energy availability, menstrual disturbance and low bone mass.
Low hydration, menstrual disturbance and muscle weakness.
High energy availability, regular menstruation and low bone mass.
Low energy availability, hypertension and muscle soreness.
feedback: The Female Athlete Triad links low energy availability, menstrual disturbance and low bone mass.

q: Menstrual stigma is most directly an issue of:
options: inclusion.
aerobic fitness.
muscular strength.
training frequency.
feedback: Stigma may create embarrassment or make participants feel unwelcome, reducing inclusion.

q: A runner tracks her menstrual cycle. Her coach automatically reduces every training session during menstruation even though she reports feeling well. Which approach would be more appropriate?
options: Reduce every session because menstrual phase always determines athletic performance.
Stop collecting menstrual-cycle information altogether.
Use her symptoms, recovery and training responses to guide adjustments appropriately.
Prevent vigorous activity throughout every phase of the menstrual cycle.
feedback: Exercise prescription should respond to the individual rather than predetermined assumptions about cycle phase.

q: A basketballer experiences fatigue and abdominal discomfort during training. She begins moving more slowly and her shooting technique becomes less consistent. Which outcome is being affected most directly?
options: Access
Inclusion
Participation
Performance
feedback: The symptoms are reducing the quality of physical and skill execution, which relates to performance.

q: A swimmer decides not to attend training because she is worried menstrual bleeding may leak through her uniform. This is primarily an effect on:
options: participation.
performance.
access to coaching.
muscular development.
feedback: She is taking part less often, so the immediate consequence is reduced participation.

q: A teenage athlete cannot afford menstrual products and therefore cannot comfortably attend weekend competition. Which issue is demonstrated most directly?
options: Access
Skill execution
Mental fitness
Coaching style
feedback: Cost is creating a practical barrier to accessing the activity.

q: Members of a sporting club regularly joke about menstruation. One athlete feels embarrassed about requesting support and believes her needs are not taken seriously. Which concept is most directly affected?
options: Inclusion
Aerobic capacity
Access to equipment
Training intensity
feedback: Negative attitudes can reduce belonging and make participants feel their needs are unwelcome.

q: An athlete experiences severe menstrual pain that repeatedly interferes with training and everyday activities. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Assume this is normal and encourage the athlete to ignore it.
Permanently remove all physical activity.
Encourage appropriate professional medical assessment and individual support.
Require the athlete to disclose the issue to teammates.
feedback: Severe or persistent symptoms should receive appropriate professional attention rather than being dismissed or managed through blanket restrictions.

q: An endurance athlete consistently consumes less energy than required for training and begins experiencing menstrual disturbance. Which additional health concern is associated with the Female Athlete Triad?
options: Reduced bone health
Improved bone density
Increased flexibility
Improved reaction time
feedback: Low energy availability can affect menstrual function and compromise bone health.

q: Which strategy would best help reduce the risk associated with the Female Athlete Triad?
options: Encourage athletes to maintain the lowest possible body weight throughout training.
Match energy intake to training demands and support healthy body-image practices.
Ignore menstrual changes unless sporting performance clearly declines.
Increase training load whenever menstrual disturbance is reported.
feedback: Adequate nutrition, healthy body image and attention to menstrual and bone health are appropriate preventative strategies.

q: A community sporting centre installs free menstrual products, private changing spaces and appropriate disposal facilities. The main purpose of these changes is to:
options: Guarantee improved performance for every participant who uses them.
Reduce practical barriers to access and participation in sport.
Identify each athlete's exact menstrual-cycle phase before training.
Replace the need for individualised physical-activity prescription.
feedback: Suitable products and facilities remove practical barriers and can make participation more manageable.

q: The AIS provides education and menstrual-health resources for athletes, coaches and health professionals. Which outcome is this most likely designed to support?
options: Support more informed and individualised responses to athletes' needs over time.
Create identical training programs for athletes at every level.
Prevent all menstrual symptoms from affecting physical activity.
Require athletes to disclose menstrual information to support staff.
feedback: Education can help athletes and support staff understand individual patterns and respond appropriately.

q: In some sporting environments, loss of menstruation was historically regarded as evidence that an athlete was training hard enough. Why is this attitude problematic?
options: Amenorrhea may signal a health concern rather than superior fitness.
Amenorrhea reliably leads to better sporting performance over the long term.
Menstrual health has little relevance to athlete wellbeing.
Loss of menstruation generally improves bone health in athletes.
feedback: Menstrual disturbance may be associated with low energy availability and other health concerns and should not be celebrated as evidence of commitment.

q: An athlete's tracking app predicts that ovulation will occur tomorrow. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The app confirms the athlete's hormone levels for that day.
The prediction is an estimate and should be considered alongside individual symptoms.
The athlete should complete the hardest training session on the predicted ovulation day.
The athlete should avoid training until the next cycle begins.
feedback: Tracking may identify patterns, but app predictions do not confirm ovulation or hormone levels.

q: An athlete records four sessions. Sessions with greater fatigue and discomfort are also the sessions in which less of the planned training is completed. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Menstruation prevents athletes from completing planned training sessions.
Higher symptoms were associated with lower completion for this athlete.
Fatigue alone explains all differences in the athlete's training completion.
Every future session should be reduced whenever symptoms are reported.
feedback: The pattern supports an individual association between symptom severity and session completion without proving a universal rule or single cause.

q: Mia reports greater fatigue than usual during training. Her diary also shows that she slept for only four hours the previous night. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Her menstrual cycle must be the only cause of fatigue.
Her sleep duration must be the only cause of fatigue.
Menstrual symptoms and other factors such as sleep should be considered.
She should stop all physical activity until the fatigue has completely disappeared.
feedback: Training responses should be interpreted individually and in context rather than attributed automatically to cycle phase.

q: A club survey identifies difficulty accessing menstrual products, embarrassment discussing menstruation and inadequate changing facilities. Which response best addresses the combination of barriers?
options: Increase training intensity to build greater resilience to discomfort.
Provide free products, suitable facilities and confidential support.
Require athletes to publicly disclose their menstrual-cycle information.
Remove athletes from activity whenever menstruation is reported.
feedback: This strategy addresses financial, practical and social barriers together.

q: A school introduces free menstrual products. Before the initiative, 24 students reported missing at least one physical-activity session because they did not have suitable products. Six months later, 8 students report the same problem. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The initiative may have reduced an access barrier.
The initiative has eliminated all barriers to physical activity.
Menstrual symptoms no longer affect any student.
Free products guarantee greater sporting performance.
feedback: The reduction is consistent with improved access, but it does not prove that every menstrual-related barrier has disappeared.

q: Over three menstrual cycles, an athlete records different levels of fatigue during the same phase each month. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: One recorded cycle can reliably predict how every future cycle will affect training.
Use patterns across cycles rather than fixed rules for each phase.
The menstrual cycle has no relevance to exercise prescription.
Training should stop whenever the same phase occurs again.
feedback: Individual experiences can vary between cycles, so repeated monitoring is more useful than fixed assumptions.

q: A professional sporting organisation has access to specialist hormone-monitoring technology, while a local community club cannot afford the same system. Which limitation does this example illustrate?
options: Hormone-monitoring technology cannot provide useful information to athletes.
Cost and specialist support can limit access to emerging technology in sport.
Community athletes do not experience meaningful hormonal changes during training.
Elite athletes no longer require individualised training programs.
feedback: Advanced technologies may improve understanding but may not be equally accessible across sporting settings.

q: A netball club provides free menstrual products but athletes still report embarrassment asking coaches for support because menstruation is regularly joked about within the team. Which additional strategy would most effectively improve the situation?
options: Remove the free menstrual products.
Introduce respectful menstrual-health education and confidential support processes.
Require all athletes to disclose their cycle publicly.
Reduce every athlete's training load.
feedback: Free products address access, but respectful education and confidential support are also needed to address stigma and inclusion.

q: An athlete cannot afford menstrual products, feels embarrassed because teammates make negative comments, misses training, and performs poorly after returning because she has completed less preparation. Which sequence best matches the four effects described?
options: Access → inclusion → participation → performance
Performance → access → inclusion → participation
Inclusion → participation → access → performance
Participation → performance → inclusion → access
feedback: Cost affects access; negative attitudes affect inclusion; missing training affects participation; reduced preparation may then affect performance.

q: Research into female athletes becomes more inclusive and coaches receive better education about menstrual health. Which future implication is most reasonable?
options: Every athlete will eventually respond to training in the same way.
Exercise prescription may become more individualised as evidence improves.
Menstrual-cycle tracking will no longer have any practical value.
Hormonal considerations will cease to affect physical activity participation.
feedback: Better research and education may allow more informed and individualised support while recognising that responses still vary.

q: A coach wants to use menstrual information to modify an athlete's training program. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Require the athlete to share cycle information with team members.
Assume cycle phase can accurately predict the athlete's performance.
With consent, privately track symptoms and adjust training when appropriate for the athlete.
Automatically remove high-intensity exercise whenever menstruation occurs.
feedback: Appropriate prescription should be consensual, private and individualised rather than based on stereotypes or compulsory disclosure.

q: Which one of the following is the best example of an acute injury?
options: Achilles pain developing gradually after repeated running.
Knee damage caused by an awkward landing.
Shoulder soreness developing after repeated swimming sessions.
Shin pain becoming progressively worse over several weeks.
feedback: Acute injuries occur during a sudden event, such as a fall, collision, awkward landing or change of direction.

q: An overuse injury is most likely to develop when:
options: body tissues are repeatedly loaded without sufficient recovery.
an athlete experiences one unexpected collision.
an athlete changes direction once during a game.
protective equipment is fitted correctly.
feedback: Overuse injuries can develop when repeated loading occurs without enough recovery time.

q: Which situation most clearly demonstrates an injury affecting access to physical activity?
options: An injured athlete feels disconnected from teammates.
A player cannot afford required rehabilitation.
Knee pain prevents an athlete from completing training.
Reduced strength slows an athlete during competition.
feedback: Cost is a practical barrier to obtaining rehabilitation and therefore affects access.

q: An injured footballer cannot compete for six weeks but continues attending team meetings and is given a role helping with drills. This strategy primarily supports the athlete's:
options: inclusion.
aerobic capacity.
injury diagnosis.
reaction time.
feedback: Maintaining contact and meaningful involvement can help an injured athlete continue to feel valued and connected.

q: A runner stops attending training because knee pain makes running uncomfortable. The injury is most directly affecting:
options: participation.
inclusion.
access to equipment.
officiating.
feedback: The athlete is taking part less often because the injury limits involvement.

q: Which statement about concussion is most accurate?
options: Loss of consciousness must occur before concussion is suspected.
Concussion can follow force to the head, neck or body during sport.
Concussion only occurs after a direct blow to the head.
An athlete without a headache cannot have concussion.
feedback: Concussion may result from force transmitted to the brain, and loss of consciousness is not required.

q: The anterior cruciate ligament assists primarily with:
options: Stabilising the knee during forward and rotational movement.
Producing energy used for muscular contraction during movement.
Absorbing impact forces through the ankle during landing.
Controlling movement at the shoulder joint during throwing.
feedback: The ACL contributes to knee stability, including control of forward movement of the shin and rotational stability.

q: Which approach is most consistent with safe participation in physical activity?
options: Increase training loads rapidly to improve adaptation.
Ignore minor warning signs until performance declines.
Match safety strategies appropriately to activity risks and individual participant needs.
Use protective equipment as the only injury-prevention strategy available.
feedback: Safety strategies should match the specific risks of the activity and the individual participant.

q: During a hockey match, Maya receives a heavy collision and appears confused and unsteady. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
options: Allow her to continue if she reports no headache.
Remove her from participation and arrange appropriate assessment.
Let her rest for five minutes and then complete a running test.
Allow her to decide whether she feels safe to continue.
feedback: Suspected concussion requires immediate removal from participation and appropriate assessment.

q: An athlete with suspected concussion feels normal again ten minutes after leaving the field. Why should the athlete still not return immediately?
options: Symptoms settling does not necessarily mean recovery is complete.
Every concussion causes permanent brain damage.
Athletes must always avoid physical activity for several months.
Feeling better proves the original symptoms were unrelated to concussion.
feedback: Symptoms can improve before recovery is complete, and returning too early may expose the athlete to further injury.

q: A concussed player returns too early and receives another heavy impact. Which consequence is most likely?
options: The second impact guarantees a faster and safer recovery.
Further injury may worsen the condition and delay recovery for the athlete.
The player automatically becomes immune to future concussion.
Continued participation reduces the need for medical assessment.
feedback: Another impact before recovery may worsen the injury and increase time away from sport.

q: A student recovering from concussion finds long periods of screen use worsen symptoms. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Complete all schoolwork without breaks.
Avoid learning permanently.
Gradually resume learning and reduce symptom-aggravating activities.
Return to unrestricted sport before returning to school.
feedback: Recovery should be gradual and individualised, including adjustments to learning where symptoms are aggravated.

q: A netballer twists awkwardly, hears a pop and develops rapid knee swelling. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Strap the knee and return if jogging feels comfortable.
Remove the athlete from play and arrange qualified assessment.
Complete several more direction changes to test stability.
Continue competing unless pain becomes severe.
feedback: A pop, swelling and instability may indicate serious injury and require removal and professional assessment.

q: Which movement is most closely associated with a possible non-contact ACL injury?
options: Controlled walking in a straight line at low speed.
Sudden direction change with poor knee control.
Seated upper-body stretching.
Standing still before competition.
feedback: ACL injuries can occur during sudden stopping, direction changes and awkward landings.

q: A basketballer repeatedly lands with the knee moving inward. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Increase the number of jumps without correcting the landing technique.
Use neuromuscular training with strength, balance and landing practice.
Avoid all jumping permanently.
Rely entirely on a knee brace.
feedback: Neuromuscular training can improve movement control through strength, balance, agility and technique practice.

q: Which statement best describes ACL injury risk?
options: A single factor explains every ACL injury that occurs in sport.
Injury risk reflects several interacting individual and environmental factors.
Female athletes will inevitably sustain ACL injuries.
Hormone levels alone determine ACL injury risk.
feedback: ACL risk can reflect interacting factors such as anatomy, movement control, strength, training opportunities and sporting environment.

q: Girls at a sporting club have limited access to strength training and receive little coaching in landing or change-of-direction technique. Why may this be relevant to injury prevention?
options: Training opportunities can influence strength and movement control.
Strength training guarantees that no knee injury will occur.
Landing technique has no relationship with knee loading.
Injury prevention is solely the athlete's responsibility.
feedback: Access to suitable training and coaching can influence modifiable factors such as strength and movement control.

q: An athlete has completed the expected rehabilitation time after an ACL injury but still lacks strength and confidence. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Time since injury alone proves the athlete is ready to compete.
Return should depend on individual recovery criteria and clinical assessment.
Confidence is unrelated to return to sport.
Competition should always resume before training.
feedback: Rehabilitation should restore physical and psychological readiness; time alone does not establish readiness.

q: Sam has returned to training following a knee injury. His leg strength remains reduced and he hesitates during direction changes. What is the most likely effect?
options: Improved skill execution.
Reduced sporting performance.
Improved access to rehabilitation.
Greater inclusion in the team.
feedback: Reduced strength and fear of reinjury may impair movement control and skill execution.

q: A rural athlete must travel several hours and pay substantial fees to receive specialist rehabilitation. This most directly demonstrates:
options: a geographic and financial access barrier.
improved inclusion.
psychological skill development.
safer officiating.
feedback: Cost and location can restrict access to appropriate recovery support.

q: Which action best reflects an athlete's responsibility for sporting safety?
options: Hiding symptoms to avoid losing selection.
Reporting injury symptoms and concerns.
Diagnosing their own concussion.
Ignoring medical advice when feeling better.
feedback: Athletes contribute to safety by reporting symptoms and injury concerns rather than concealing them.

q: A coach notices that an injured player is being pressured by teammates to return before medical clearance. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Encourage the athlete to play through the injury.
Prioritise athlete welfare and support appropriate recovery.
Allow teammates to decide whether the athlete returns.
Ignore the situation because safety is solely the athlete's responsibility.
feedback: Coaches should provide safe preparation and avoid pressuring athletes to continue when injured.

q: A sports club records 18 injury presentations for ages 8–9, 42 for ages 10–14, 37 for ages 15–19 and 25 for ages 20–24. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The 10–14 group recorded the most injury presentations.
Injury risk always decreases with age.
Every participant aged 10–14 will experience a sports injury.
Age is the only factor influencing injury.
feedback: The data support a comparison of the recorded groups but do not establish universal injury risk or prove a single cause.

q: A coach records increasingly high training loads alongside increasing athlete fatigue over four weeks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Continue increasing training load regardless of reported fatigue.
Review training load and allow adequate recovery.
Eliminate all future training.
Assume the athlete has a concussion.
feedback: Gradual training progression and adequate recovery are strategies used to reduce injury risk.

q: During rehabilitation, an athlete's leg strength improves from 60% to 90% of pre-injury level, confidence improves, and change-of-direction control improves. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Rehabilitation has improved several indicators of readiness.
The athlete is automatically ready for competition.
Confidence is the only factor relevant to return.
Time since injury is the only necessary criterion.
feedback: Strength, movement control and confidence have improved, although return should still follow appropriate individual assessment.

q: A team introduces a warm-up containing lower-body strength, balance, agility and controlled landing activities. Knee injuries decrease during the following season. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The program may have reduced modifiable injury risk.
The program guarantees no future knee injury will occur.
Protective equipment is now unnecessary in every sport.
Every knee injury has the same cause.
feedback: Neuromuscular programs can reduce modifiable risk, but no program can prevent every injury.

q: A professional club uses cryotherapy and dynamic air compression, while a community club cannot afford either technique. What issue does this demonstrate?
options: Recovery resources may differ between sporting settings.
Community athletes do not require recovery.
Expensive technology guarantees better outcomes.
Injury management is unrelated to financial resources.
feedback: Some recovery technologies are more accessible to organisations with greater financial resources.

q: Before concussion education, 14 athletes reported that they would continue playing after feeling dizzy following a collision. After education, only 4 reported that they would continue. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Education may have improved appropriate withdrawal from play.
Education eliminates all concussions.
Dizziness is unrelated to concussion.
Education proves that injury rates will fall to zero.
feedback: Education can improve awareness and willingness to respond appropriately, although it cannot eliminate all injury.

q: An injured netballer cannot afford private physiotherapy, feels disconnected after missing team activities, attends fewer training sessions and moves more slowly after returning. Which sequence correctly identifies the effects?
options: Access → inclusion → participation → performance
Inclusion → access → performance → participation
Participation → performance → access → inclusion
Performance → inclusion → access → participation
feedback: Rehabilitation cost affects access; disconnection affects inclusion; fewer sessions affects participation; slower movement affects performance.

q: A junior sporting league introduces a rule requiring athletes with suspected concussion to be removed from play, assessed appropriately and complete a gradual return process. How is this most likely to reduce the impact of injury?
options: It guarantees that concussion will never occur.
It reduces continued participation during possible recovery.
It allows athletes to return as soon as symptoms briefly disappear.
It places all responsibility for concussion on the athlete.
feedback: Removal and controlled return reduce exposure to further injury during recovery and place athlete welfare ahead of immediate performance.

q: Historically, athletes were sometimes praised for 'playing through pain'. Current sporting practice increasingly encourages injury reporting and appropriate assessment. What does this change most clearly demonstrate?
options: A shift toward prioritising athlete welfare over toughness in sport.
A reduction in the importance of participant safety.
A return to earlier sporting attitudes.
An expectation that athletes diagnose their own injuries.
feedback: Current approaches increasingly prioritise athlete wellbeing rather than treating continued participation while injured as evidence of toughness.

q: A soccer club wants to reduce lower-limb injuries. It introduces strength and movement training but makes no changes to an unsafe playing surface. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The program is sufficient because strength training removes every injury risk.
The strategy addresses some risks but not environmental hazards.
Playing surfaces cannot influence injury.
The club should stop strength training completely.
feedback: Injury prevention should address relevant individual and environmental risks rather than relying on one strategy alone.

q: An athlete has completed several weeks of intense training and reports high fatigue but no specific injury. Which strategy is most appropriate for reducing injury risk?
options: Increase training volume further.
Allow adequate rest and recovery to manage fatigue.
Avoid all nutrition following training.
Wait until an injury develops before changing the program.
feedback: Adequate recovery can reduce fatigue and the risk of injuries associated with excessive training load.

q: An elite athlete has immediate access to medical staff and specialist rehabilitation technology after injury, while a community athlete has limited local services. Which conclusion best reflects this comparison?
options: Injury management resources can vary considerably between sporting settings.
Community athletes experience less serious injuries.
Elite injury-management strategies are automatically appropriate for every community club.
Access to support has no influence on recovery.
feedback: Access to specialist rehabilitation and recovery resources can vary considerably between elite and community sporting settings.

q: Future injury-management technology becomes more effective but remains expensive. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Innovation will automatically improve safety equally for every participant.
New technology may help, but cost can restrict access across sporting settings.
Traditional prevention strategies will become unnecessary.
Community clubs will no longer need coach education.
feedback: Future developments may improve prevention and rehabilitation, but strategies also need to be practical, affordable and accessible.

q: Which statement best describes confidence in relation to physical activity and sport?
options: The ability to maintain the same training load in every situation.
Belief in your ability to succeed or perform effectively.
The amount of enjoyment gained from an activity.
The ability to ignore feedback from others.
feedback: Confidence involves belief in your ability to succeed. It can influence whether someone is willing to begin, continue or perform an activity.

q: Which example best demonstrates intrinsic motivation?
options: Exercising to receive a prize.
Training because a coach has threatened extra work.
Participating because the activity is enjoyable and personally satisfying.
Playing sport only to gain social-media attention.
feedback: Intrinsic motivation comes from internal enjoyment or satisfaction rather than external rewards or pressure.

q: Concentration is best described as:
options: focusing attention on information that is relevant to the task.
increasing physical activation before every activity.
believing that success is guaranteed.
reducing the amount of sleep required before an important competition.
feedback: Concentration involves directing attention towards relevant cues, instructions and feedback.

q: Which statement about optimal arousal is most accurate?
options: Every athlete performs best at the same level of arousal.
The highest possible level of arousal produces the best performance.
Optimal arousal refers only to physical activation.
The ideal level of arousal varies between individuals and activities.
feedback: Optimal arousal is the level of physical and mental activation that best suits the individual and the task.

q: Which statement best explains sleep optimisation?
options: Reducing sleep so more time is available for training.
Using habits and opportunities that support sufficient, good-quality sleep.
Sleeping for exactly the same number of hours as every other athlete.
Replacing recovery activities with daytime naps.
feedback: Sleep optimisation involves creating conditions and routines that support adequate sleep quality and duration.

q: Mental imagery involves:
options: analysing written performance statistics.
increasing physical training volume immediately before competition to improve sporting performance.
mentally rehearsing an action or situation without physically performing it.
avoiding thoughts about an upcoming performance.
feedback: Imagery involves mentally rehearsing movements, sensations or situations and can support confidence and concentration.

q: Which example best demonstrates positive or instructional self-talk?
options: Stay balanced and watch the ball.
Everyone else is better than me.
If I miss this, the match is over.
I always make mistakes under pressure.
feedback: Helpful self-talk uses realistic statements or cue words to direct attention and reinforce confidence or technique.

q: Progressive muscle relaxation involves:
options: completing repeated high-intensity movements.
visualising a successful performance.
repeating a motivational phrase.
deliberately tensing and then releasing muscle groups to reduce physical tension.
feedback: Progressive muscle relaxation helps an athlete recognise and reduce excessive muscular tension.

q: A student wants to join a recreational swimming program but worries that they will be slower than everyone else and decides not to attend. Which strategy would be most appropriate?
options: Place the student immediately in the most advanced training group.
Tell the student that confidence should not influence participation.
Provide an achievable introductory challenge and supportive feedback about progress.
Require the student to compete before attending regular sessions.
feedback: Achievable early success and supportive feedback can strengthen confidence and make beginning an unfamiliar activity more manageable.

q: A community fitness program wants to improve participants' motivation to continue attending. Which strategy best supports autonomy?
options: Require every participant to complete an identical program.
Allow participants to choose between suitable activities and difficulty levels.
Remove all opportunities for participants to set their own personal goals.
Increase external rewards after every session.
feedback: Meaningful choice can increase a participant's sense of control and strengthen motivation to continue.

q: A new volleyball player listens carefully to instructions, responds to teammates and applies coaching feedback. Which outcome is most directly supported?
options: Reduced access to the activity because training feels more difficult.
Increased physical arousal.
Reduced need for practice.
Improved skill learning and stronger connection with teammates.
feedback: Concentration supports learning and communication, which can improve skill development and a sense of belonging.

q: A basketballer becomes highly anxious before taking a free throw. Their breathing becomes rapid and their muscles feel tense. Which strategy is most appropriate immediately before the shot?
options: Controlled breathing.
Increasing training volume.
Reviewing several pages of statistics.
Focusing on the consequences of missing.
feedback: Controlled breathing can reduce excessive physical and psychological arousal and help the athlete refocus on the task.

q: A diver has learned a new skill but feels uncertain before competition. Which use of imagery would be most appropriate?
options: Imagine the consequences of making an error.
Replace all physical practice with visualisation.
Mentally rehearse the approach, take-off and successful execution of the skill.
Avoid thinking about the skill until the competition begins that day.
feedback: Rehearsing successful execution can reinforce confidence and direct attention towards relevant technique.

q: After making two passing errors, a footballer begins thinking, 'I'm ruining the game.' Which response would best help the athlete refocus?
options: Increase concern about the final score and possible consequences of making another passing error under pressure.
Use a short cue such as 'next pass' and focus on the next relevant action.
Stop communicating with teammates.
Avoid attempting another pass.
feedback: Helpful self-talk and task-relevant cues can redirect attention away from the previous error and towards the next action.

q: An athlete regularly obtains insufficient sleep before early-morning training. Which effect is most likely?
options: Improved concentration because the athlete becomes accustomed to fatigue.
Faster recovery because less time is spent asleep.
Improved skill accuracy because more time is available for training.
Reduced concentration, decision-making and physical recovery.
feedback: Insufficient sleep can impair concentration, decision-making, skill execution and recovery.

q: Which strategy would most appropriately support sleep hygiene?
options: Maintaining a consistent sleep routine and reducing stimulating activity close to bedtime.
Consuming caffeine immediately before bed.
Increasing screen use when trying to fall asleep.
Completing intense exercise whenever the athlete wakes during the night to become tired again.
feedback: Consistent routines, reduced stimulation and a suitable sleep environment can support sleep quality.

q: An athlete's wearable device gives a low readiness score, but the athlete reports feeling well and has completed training normally. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Cancel all physical activity because the device is always accurate.
Ignore all sleep-monitoring information.
Consider the readiness score alongside the athlete's symptoms, recovery and training responses.
Use the score to prescribe the same training reduction for every athlete.
feedback: Wearable data can identify patterns, but estimates should be interpreted alongside individual feedback and performance information.

q: An elite competition repeatedly schedules matches that finish very late at night. How could this influence athletes?
options: Late matches automatically improve performance.
Reduced sleep opportunity may affect recovery, concentration and preparation for later competition.
Athletes no longer require recovery after late matches.
Match scheduling cannot influence an athlete's sleep.
feedback: Late finishes, travel and post-event recovery routines can reduce sleep opportunities and affect readiness.

q: An athlete reports low confidence but is not experiencing excessive tension or anxiety. Which strategy would be most appropriate?
options: Increase physiological arousal as much as possible.
Reduce sleep before competition.
Ignore the athlete's concerns.
Use successful imagery and realistic positive self-talk.
feedback: Imagery and helpful self-talk can reinforce preparation and confidence when low self-belief is the main difficulty.

q: A beginner attends training with a friend who provides encouragement and helps them understand the session. What is the most likely effect?
options: Greater confidence and a stronger likelihood of continuing participation.
Reduced inclusion because relying on a friend prevents independent participation in the program.
Reduced intrinsic motivation in every situation.
Greater sleep disturbance.
feedback: Encouragement and social support can strengthen confidence, belonging and commitment to continued participation.

q: An athlete records the following passing results: 6 hours sleep = 64% successful passes; 7 hours = 72%; 8 hours = 80%; 9 hours = 81%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Every extra hour of sleep produces exactly an 8% improvement in performance.
Greater sleep duration was associated with improved passing accuracy for this athlete.
Nine hours of sleep guarantees peak performance for every athlete.
Sleep duration was the only factor affecting passing accuracy.
feedback: The data show an association for this athlete, but they do not establish a universal rule or prove causation.

q: Across four sessions, an athlete records: 5.5 hours sleep, fatigue 8/10, 45 of 75 minutes completed; 7.5 hours, fatigue 4/10, 70 of 75 minutes; 8 hours, fatigue 3/10, 75 of 75 minutes; 6 hours, fatigue 7/10, 50 of 75 minutes. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Sleep duration is proven to be the only factor determining whether the athlete completes each session.
Every athlete should sleep for exactly eight hours.
The athlete should permanently reduce all sessions to 50 minutes.
Lower sleep duration and higher fatigue were associated with reduced session completion for this athlete.
feedback: The pattern supports an association between sleep, fatigue and training completion, but other influences may also contribute.

q: During competition, an athlete shows rapid breathing, tense shoulders, difficulty concentrating and rushed decisions. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The athlete is under-aroused and requires greater stimulation to improve concentration.
The athlete's confidence must be high.
The athlete may be experiencing excessive arousal that is reducing performance.
The athlete is demonstrating optimal concentration.
feedback: Excessive arousal can involve tension, worry and reduced concentration, which may contribute to rushed decisions and poorer execution.

q: A tennis player loses three consecutive points and begins thinking about the previous mistakes instead of watching the opponent. Which strategy would best address the immediate problem?
options: Use a simple attentional cue such as 'watch the ball' before the next point.
Increase concern about the previous points.
Stop using feedback during the match.
Reduce sleep the night before the next competition so the athlete feels more alert and focused.
feedback: A task-relevant cue can redirect concentration towards information needed for the next action.

q: A professional sporting organisation employs a full-time sport psychologist and sleep specialist. A small community club relies mainly on volunteer coaches and free online resources. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Community athletes do not require psychological support.
Access to specialised psychological and sleep support can differ between sporting settings.
Professional support guarantees better performance.
Online education removes every difference in access to specialised psychological and sleep support across sporting settings.
feedback: Financial and organisational resources can influence access to specialist psychological and sleep support.

q: A beginner attends a group exercise session but feels uncomfortable because they have little experience. The instructor provides a choice of activities, sets an achievable first goal and gives supportive feedback. Which outcome is most likely?
options: The participant will become dependent on external rewards.
The participant's concentration will necessarily decrease.
The participant will no longer need further practice.
Increased confidence and autonomy may support continued participation.
feedback: Achievable success and meaningful choice can strengthen confidence and motivation, making continued participation more likely.

q: Before a gymnastics routine, an athlete experiences excessive arousal and muscle tension. Which sequence best explains how an appropriate strategy could improve performance?
options: Controlled breathing → reduced tension → improved concentration → more controlled skill execution.
Reduced sleep → increased fatigue → improved concentration → better execution.
Negative self-talk → increased doubt → improved confidence → better execution.
Greater worry → increased arousal → improved decision-making → better execution.
feedback: Controlled breathing can reduce excessive arousal, allowing the athlete to focus more effectively and execute skills with greater control.

q: A sporting academy introduces wearable devices that estimate sleep duration, sleep quality and readiness. Coaches plan to use the readiness score to determine each athlete's training load. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The score should replace all communication with athletes.
The technology guarantees accurate training prescription.
The data may support individualised decisions, but should be interpreted alongside athlete feedback and other performance information.
Every athlete with the same readiness score should complete an identical program.
feedback: Monitoring technology can provide useful information, but estimates have limitations and should not replace individual assessment.

q: Which statement best describes a change in the use of psychological skills in sport?
options: Psychological preparation has become less important as physical training has improved.
Psychological skills and sleep are increasingly treated as part of overall athlete preparation alongside physical training.
Current sporting practice increasingly discourages athletes from using imagery, concentration and self-talk strategies during important competitive performances.
Sleep is now considered unrelated to recovery.
feedback: Contemporary approaches increasingly integrate psychological preparation, sleep and physical training as parts of athlete performance and wellbeing.

q: An international sporting event schedules several matches late at night to maximise television audiences. Athletes report difficulty obtaining adequate sleep before their next matches. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: Audience size should always take priority over athlete recovery.
Late scheduling cannot influence performance if athletes are elite.
Athletes should simply reduce their need for sleep.
Organisers should consider commercial demands alongside athletes' sleep opportunity, recovery and wellbeing.
feedback: Event scheduling can affect sleep and recovery, so athlete wellbeing should be considered alongside commercial and audience demands.

q: Which statement best describes mental fitness?
options: Mental fitness means never experiencing stress, disappointment or psychological difficulty during sport.
Skills and habits that help people cope with challenges and support wellbeing.
The ability to ignore stress during competition.
A measure of physical strength and endurance.
feedback: Mental fitness involves skills that support coping and wellbeing. It does not mean a person will never experience mental-health difficulties.

q: Which of the following is a component of mental fitness?
options: Maximum aerobic capacity.
Reaction time.
Emotional resilience.
Flexibility.
feedback: Emotional resilience is one component of mental fitness and involves adapting to setbacks and difficulties.

q: Cognitive functioning most directly involves:
options: thinking, learning, decision-making and problem-solving.
muscular strength, power and endurance.
access to sporting facilities.
competition scheduling.
feedback: Cognitive functioning supports attention, learning, decision-making and problem-solving.

q: How can social connection contribute to mental fitness?
options: By removing the need for recovery.
By guaranteeing improved sporting performance.
By preventing all stress.
By providing belonging, support and meaningful relationships.
feedback: Supportive relationships can provide belonging and help people cope with challenges.

q: Which statement about physical activity and mental fitness is most accurate?
options: Physical activity prevents all mental illness when people participate frequently enough in organised sport programs.
Physical activity may support mood, coping and social connection, but benefits vary between individuals.
Only competitive sport can support mental fitness.
Physical activity removes the need for professional support.
feedback: Physical activity can support wellbeing, but outcomes vary and some people may also require professional support.

q: Which strategy is most directly associated with managing stress in sport?
options: Increasing training whenever an athlete experiences competitive stress.
Avoiding all competition.
Using controlled breathing or mindfulness to manage pressure.
Ignoring signs of fatigue.
feedback: Controlled breathing and mindfulness can help athletes manage physical tension and focus on the present moment.

q: Emotional resilience is best described as:
options: the ability to adapt constructively to setbacks and challenges.
never experiencing disappointment.
avoiding situations where failure is possible.
maintaining the same emotional response in every challenging situation.
feedback: Resilience involves acknowledging setbacks and responding constructively rather than avoiding all difficulty.

q: An elite sport pathway is most likely to include:
options: only recreational physical activity.
informal games with no organised coaching.
activities designed solely for beginners.
academies, representative squads and specialised development programs.
feedback: Elite pathways support athletes progressing towards higher levels through specialised coaching and development opportunities.

q: A beginner stops attending a fitness program after making several mistakes during the first session. Which strategy would most appropriately support continued participation?
options: Increase the difficulty immediately.
Tell the participant mistakes should never occur.
Set achievable challenges and provide constructive feedback about progress.
Compare the participant publicly with the strongest member of the group.
feedback: Achievable challenges and constructive feedback can support confidence, motivation and willingness to continue.

q: A community walking group wants new participants to feel more included. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Require every participant to exercise alone throughout the entire program.
Create welcoming group activities and opportunities for participants to interact.
Remove all beginner sessions.
Rank participants according to speed.
feedback: Meaningful interaction and a shared purpose can strengthen social connection and belonging.

q: A person wants to become active but is unsure what local opportunities are available. Which strategy would most directly improve access?
options: Increase training intensity.
Require specialist equipment before joining.
Reduce the number of available programs so participants have fewer choices to consider.
Provide clear information about location, cost, activity type and available support.
feedback: Accessible information can reduce uncertainty and help people identify suitable opportunities.

q: A participant joins a recreational basketball program, enjoys learning new skills and develops new friendships. Which mental-fitness benefits are most clearly demonstrated?
options: Achievement and social connection.
Increased physiological arousal only.
Reduced access to activity.
Elimination of all future stress.
feedback: Skill development can provide achievement, while shared activity can strengthen social connection.

q: Which approach is most likely to support a positive physical-activity experience?
options: Requiring everyone to perform at the same level.
Using public comparison to increase pressure.
Providing choice, achievable challenge and a supportive environment.
Discouraging beginners from asking for help.
feedback: Choice, achievable success and supportive environments can strengthen enjoyment and continued participation.

q: An athlete is struggling to balance training, schoolwork and recovery and is becoming increasingly stressed. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Add extra training sessions so the athlete becomes more accustomed to competing under pressure.
Review the schedule and plan time for training, schoolwork and recovery.
Stop communicating with support people.
Ignore the issue unless performance declines.
feedback: Planning and workload management can help athletes manage competing demands.

q: An athlete is not selected for a representative team. Which response best demonstrates emotional resilience?
options: Stop participating permanently.
Blame teammates for the decision.
Avoid asking for feedback.
Acknowledge the disappointment, seek constructive feedback and set achievable improvement goals.
feedback: Resilience involves responding constructively to setbacks and identifying appropriate next steps.

q: During a match, a footballer notices an unmarked teammate and quickly selects an appropriate pass. Which component of mental fitness is most directly involved?
options: Cognitive functioning.
Social exclusion.
Structural access.
Physical strength.
feedback: Cognitive functioning supports information processing, decision-making and problem-solving during performance.

q: An athlete in a development pathway is experiencing ongoing difficulties but worries that asking for help will affect selection. Which organisational response is most appropriate?
options: Tell athletes that seeking professional help demonstrates a lack of commitment to their sporting pathway.
Require concerns to be discussed publicly.
Provide confidential support options and clear referral pathways that do not unfairly penalise help-seeking.
Remove the athlete from the pathway immediately.
feedback: Supportive help-seeking cultures reduce fear and make appropriate assistance easier to access.

q: An athlete tells a coach they are experiencing significant ongoing psychological difficulties. What is the most appropriate role for the coach?
options: Diagnose the athlete's condition based on the coach's own observations and previous sporting experience alone.
Listen, provide appropriate support and connect the athlete with qualified professional help when needed.
Provide treatment without specialist support.
Ignore the issue unless performance changes.
feedback: Coaches can support athletes and facilitate referral, but diagnosis and treatment should be provided by appropriately qualified professionals.

q: An academy athlete reports persistent fatigue, poor concentration and reduced enjoyment after several weeks of increased training and travel. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Increase the athlete's workload further so greater training exposure builds resilience to fatigue.
Remove all recovery opportunities.
Assume the athlete lacks motivation.
Review training and travel demands and adjust workload and recovery where appropriate.
feedback: Monitoring and adjusting workload can address fatigue and support wellbeing and continued participation.

q: A development program changes training times every week with little notice. Athletes struggle to plan schoolwork and sleep. This example best demonstrates:
options: organisational decisions influencing individual wellbeing and participation.
an athlete's fitness level determining program access.
mental fitness eliminating environmental barriers.
a purely intrapersonal issue.
feedback: Organisational conditions such as scheduling can influence fatigue, concentration, motivation and participation.

q: An academy records the following observations over four weeks: Week 1—moderate workload, low fatigue; Week 2—moderate workload, low fatigue; Week 3—high workload, high fatigue; Week 4—high workload, reduced enjoyment and concentration. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: High workload always causes poor mental health.
The athlete should stop training permanently.
Increased workload was associated with greater fatigue and reduced enjoyment and concentration in this case.
Training workload cannot influence mental fitness.
feedback: The pattern shows an association in this case but does not prove that workload is the only influence.

q: A survey of academy athletes finds that 72% know where to access support, 38% believe asking for help may affect selection, and 31% say they would speak to their coach about a wellbeing concern. Which action would most directly address the identified barrier?
options: Increase training demands.
Strengthen confidential support processes and reassure athletes that appropriate help-seeking will not unfairly affect selection.
Require athletes to publicly disclose wellbeing concerns so coaches can monitor every issue affecting selection decisions.
Remove support services from the academy.
feedback: Fear of selection consequences is a barrier to help-seeking, so confidential and fair support processes directly address that concern.

q: Participants in a community program report greater enjoyment after six weeks, increased social connection and improved confidence in completing activities. Some participants still require professional mental-health support. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Physical activity has cured all mental-health difficulties.
Professional support is unnecessary once activity begins.
Social connection has no meaningful relationship with mental fitness, wellbeing or continued participation in community physical activity programs.
Physical activity may support several aspects of mental fitness while some people still require additional professional support.
feedback: Physical activity can support wellbeing, confidence and connection without replacing professional care when it is needed.

q: An elite volleyball program adds two late-night training sessions each week. An athlete subsequently reports fatigue and difficulty concentrating at school. Which relationship is most accurately described?
options: The organisational training schedule may influence the athlete's fatigue and concentration.
Fatigue is solely an organisational factor.
Concentration cannot be affected by scheduling.
The athlete's response proves that late training is unsuitable for every athlete.
feedback: Organisational conditions can influence intrapersonal responses such as fatigue and concentration.

q: A metropolitan academy employs psychologists, dietitians and welfare staff. A smaller regional program has one coach and relies on external community services. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Regional athletes do not require mental fitness support because smaller programs involve less pressure and stress.
Specialist support guarantees better performance.
Access to specialist mental-fitness support may differ between sporting pathways and locations.
Community services cannot support athletes.
feedback: Resources and location can influence access to specialist support across different sporting environments.

q: An elite swimmer attends early-morning training three times each week, reports persistent fatigue and is struggling to concentrate at school. The athlete fears that asking for fewer sessions may affect selection. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Require the athlete to continue the same workload because reducing training may weaken commitment to the pathway.
Consult with the athlete, review the training schedule and adjust workload or recovery opportunities where appropriate.
Tell the athlete that fatigue is solely their responsibility.
Remove the athlete from the pathway.
feedback: Reviewing workload is within the pathway's control and can address fatigue while respecting the athlete's individual needs.

q: Which sequence best explains how an organisational decision may influence participation?
options: Reduced sleep → unpredictable schedule → improved motivation → increased participation.
Improved belonging → unequal support → reduced confidence → increased participation.
Unpredictable scheduling → reduced recovery → fatigue and lower motivation → reduced participation.
Higher workload → greater fatigue → guaranteed improved performance → increased overall participation.
feedback: Organisational scheduling can influence recovery and individual responses, which may then affect willingness or ability to participate.

q: Athletes in an elite pathway report anxiety, fatigue and uncertainty about where to seek help. Which strategy best demonstrates organisational responsibility?
options: Leave all wellbeing decisions to individual athletes.
Require coaches to diagnose psychological conditions.
Focus only on competition results.
Provide regular private check-ins, monitor workload and recovery, and establish clear professional referral pathways.
feedback: Elite pathways share responsibility for athlete wellbeing through practical support, monitoring and appropriate referral systems.

q: Which statement best describes a change in attitudes towards mental fitness in sport?
options: Sport has increasingly shifted from viewing help-seeking as weakness towards recognising wellbeing and support as part of athlete development.
Modern sport places less emphasis on athlete wellbeing because successful performance is now considered more important than psychological support, recovery and help-seeking.
Current approaches discourage athletes from discussing difficulties.
Mental fitness is now considered relevant only after problems occur.
feedback: Contemporary approaches increasingly recognise mental fitness, early support and help-seeking as important parts of athlete development.

q: A national sporting organisation plans to introduce online mental-fitness education and regular wellbeing check-ins across development pathways. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: Online delivery will automatically provide equal access to every athlete.
Regular check-ins remove the need for professional referral.
The approach may improve early support and access, but connectivity, privacy, cost and effectiveness should still be evaluated.
Mental-fitness education should replace physical training.
feedback: Future strategies may improve access and early support, but practical issues such as privacy, connectivity and effectiveness must still be considered.

q: A local council provides free menstrual products in community sporting facilities. What is the most likely benefit?
options: It ensures every participant will experience improved sporting performance.
It removes the need for clubs to provide inclusive changing facilities.
It prevents menstrual symptoms from affecting physical activity.
It reduces a practical barrier that may limit access and participation.
feedback: Providing free menstrual products can reduce a practical and financial barrier to accessing and participating in physical activity.

q: Why is increased research involving female athletes important for physical-activity prescription?
options: It allows one training program to be prescribed for all female athletes.
It proves menstrual-cycle phase is the main influence on sporting performance.
It can improve evidence used to develop more individualised exercise programs.
It removes the need to consider an athlete's symptoms and training responses.
feedback: Better research can improve understanding of individual responses and support more informed physical-activity prescription.

q: Two athletes are in the same menstrual-cycle phase. One reports feeling well, while the other reports significant fatigue and discomfort. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Give both athletes the same reduced training program.
Prevent both athletes from completing vigorous physical activity.
Ignore their symptoms because they are in the same cycle phase.
Adjust training according to each athlete's symptoms and responses.
feedback: Physical-activity prescription should consider individual symptoms and responses rather than assuming all athletes respond identically.

q: A coach wants athletes to record menstrual information to help guide training. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Require every athlete to display their information to the team.
Use the information to predict performance without consulting athletes.
Share individual records with other coaches whenever requested.
Make participation voluntary and keep relevant information private.
feedback: Menstrual information should be handled respectfully, with consent and appropriate privacy.

q: Advanced hormone-monitoring technology may provide additional information for exercise prescription. Which limitation should sporting organisations consider?
options: The technology means athlete feedback is no longer useful.
The technology guarantees accurate performance predictions.
Cost and specialist expertise may limit equitable access.
The technology removes the need for individualised programs.
feedback: Emerging technology may offer benefits, but cost and access to specialist expertise can limit its availability across sporting settings.

q: A sporting organisation reduces menstrual stigma through education, but some participants still cannot afford menstrual products. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The strategy has removed every barrier affecting participation.
The education is ineffective because performance has not been measured.
The organisation should stop discussing menstrual health.
The strategy may improve inclusion, while an access barrier remains.
feedback: Education may reduce stigma and improve inclusion, but financial barriers can still restrict access and participation.

q: Which response is most appropriate when concussion is suspected during sport?
options: Allow the athlete to continue if symptoms appear mild.
Complete a fitness test before deciding whether to continue.
Remove the athlete from participation and arrange appropriate assessment.
Wait until the following day before responding to the symptoms.
feedback: An athlete with suspected concussion should be removed from participation and appropriately assessed.

q: A club wants to reduce knee injuries. Which strategy provides the most comprehensive approach?
options: Provide knee braces to every participant regardless of individual need.
Focus only on increasing the amount of training completed each week.
Replace strength training with additional competitive matches.
Combine movement training with appropriate environmental and safety checks.
feedback: Effective injury prevention can address both participant-related factors and environmental risks.

q: Why should return to sport after injury not be based only on the amount of time that has passed?
options: All athletes recover from the same injury at exactly the same rate.
Time since injury is unrelated to rehabilitation in every situation.
Physical and psychological readiness should also be assessed.
Returning later always guarantees that reinjury will not occur.
feedback: Return-to-sport decisions should consider individual recovery, including physical function and psychological readiness.

q: A rural sporting club introduces telehealth physiotherapy and subsidised travel for injured athletes who need specialist care. What is the main purpose of these strategies?
options: Increase the intensity of rehabilitation programs.
Ensure athletes return to competition immediately.
Replace all face-to-face health services in rural communities.
Reduce geographic and financial barriers to rehabilitation.
feedback: Travel distance and cost can restrict access to rehabilitation, so these strategies aim to reduce those barriers.

q: Why might an independent medical professional be used to assess a suspected concussion during elite sport?
options: To guarantee the athlete will be cleared to return immediately.
To transfer responsibility for safety entirely to the athlete.
To reduce potential conflicts between player welfare and competitive pressures during assessment.
To allow coaches to make the final medical diagnosis.
feedback: Independent assessment can help ensure decisions prioritise athlete welfare rather than competitive pressures.

q: What is a likely benefit of national concussion guidelines for community sport?
options: They eliminate the possibility of concussion occurring.
They allow every sport to ignore its own participation risks.
They guarantee identical recovery times for every athlete.
They promote more consistent recognition and management of concussion.
feedback: National guidance can support more consistent safety practices while individual recovery still needs to be considered.

q: Future wearable technology may help monitor training load and possible injury risk. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Wearable technology will prevent every sporting injury from occurring.
Technology should replace coaches and qualified health professionals.
It can support decisions when used with other relevant information and professional judgement.
Anyone using wearable technology can safely increase training without limits.
feedback: Technology may provide useful information, but injury-prevention decisions should consider multiple sources of evidence and professional judgement.

q: A team reports increasing fatigue during a heavy training block, and coaches also identify an uneven playing surface. Which response best addresses injury risk?
options: Continue the training load because no injury has occurred yet.
Repair the surface but make no changes to recovery practices.
Reduce training but continue using the unsafe playing surface.
Review training and recovery while also correcting the environmental hazard.
feedback: A comprehensive injury-prevention approach addresses both training-related and environmental risk factors.
